solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Comparatively brave to tackle what one observes

indicators.note: to tackle something is to grab hold of it, so one piece wraps itself around another

blocks.note: the comparative form of bold
eh? is a way of saying 'what?' when you have not heard

explanation.surface: Someone braver than you takes on whatever they happen to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What one observes' reads as one phrase, but 'what' belongs to the wordplay as the interjection eh?, and the definition is only 'one observes'.
explanation.definitionFit: A beholder is a person who watches or sees, as in the saying about beauty and the eye.

clue.text: Got mechanical part inside buzzer

indicators.note: inside places one thing within the walls of another

blocks.note: a bee is an insect that buzzes
a cam is a rotating machine part that drives a follower

explanation.surface: Someone discovers a mechanical component lodged in a doorbell or alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: The buzzer looks like an electric device, but in crosswords it is usually the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: Got in the sense of 'got angry' means grew or turned into, which is what became expresses.

clue.text: Possess many great properties as one contracting auctioneer does

blocks.note: first meaning: to be well endowed with good qualities
second meaning: an auctioneer under contract puts a lot, an item for sale, up for bids

explanation.surface: An estate agent boasts about grand houses while signing up an auctioneer.
explanation.walkthrough: Properties suggests real estate, but here it means qualities; the auctioneer's sense turns on 'lot' as a numbered item put up for sale.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone with plenty of good qualities, and literally describes an auctioneer presenting an item for bidding.

clue.text: Transport fifty soldiers on railway

blocks.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
RY is a standard abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: Fifty troops are moved by train.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene is about moving troops by rail, but the soldiers and railway are only abbreviations; a lorry is the British word for a truck.
explanation.definitionFit: A lorry is a large goods vehicle, so it is a means of transport for freight.

clue.text: Stretch of river blocked by vessels

indicators.note: something blocked has an obstruction sitting in its middle

blocks.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, a favourite crossword river
pans are cooking vessels

explanation.surface: Boats are blocking a section of river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stretch of river' reads as one phrase, but the definition ends at 'Stretch'; the vessels are cooking pans, not boats.
explanation.definitionFit: An expanse is a wide, open area, the same as a stretch of land or water.

clue.text: We should split sacks

blocks.note: first meaning: a call to leave together, split being slang for depart
second meaning: dismisses an employee from a job

explanation.surface: Someone suggests the group divide up the bags between them.
explanation.walkthrough: Split looks like dividing, and sacks look like bags; both are verbs, one for leaving and one for firing.
explanation.definitionFit: The contraction urges a group to leave, and the verb phrase means dismisses a worker from employment.

clue.text: Name half-hearted novelist that’s turned dynamic

indicators.note: with only half a heart, one of the two central letters goes missing
turned round, the string now runs back to front

blocks.note: to cite is to name or mention
Graham Greene, with one of the double E at its centre dropped

explanation.surface: A writer who has lost enthusiasm somehow becomes lively again.
explanation.walkthrough: Name is a verb giving CITE, not N; GREENE's heart is its middle pair EE, and losing half of it leaves GRENE. CITEGRENE read backwards is ENERGETIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Dynamic and energetic are synonyms, both describing someone full of drive and vigour.

clue.text: Unfulfilled aspirations matter, she dreads failing

indicators.note: something failing is going wrong and breaking down, so the letters fall apart and regroup

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Thwarted ambitions count, a woman fears, as she worries about failure.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is all fifteen letters of 'matter, she dreads'; the comma only serves the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopes that come to nothing are described idiomatically as broken or ruined dreams.

clue.text: Reject concerning temptation to change sides

indicators.note: sides are left and right, so the letter for one is swapped for the letter for the other

blocks.note: over can mean about or concerning, as in a row over money
a lure is a temptation or enticement

explanation.surface: Someone rejects talk of being tempted to defect to the other party.
explanation.walkthrough: L and R are the abbreviations for left and right; turning the L of LURE into R gives RULE.
explanation.definitionFit: To overrule is to set aside or reverse a decision, as a judge rejects an objection.

clue.text: Chap to incite revolutionary conspiracies

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: cove is old British slang for a man or fellow
to spur is to urge on or incite

explanation.surface: A man stirs up a revolution through plotting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary conspiracies' reads as one phrase about plotters, but revolutionary turns the incite word round.
explanation.definitionFit: Cover-ups are schemes to conceal wrongdoing, and are often the product of conspiracies.

clue.text: Ambassador dined after part of journey

indicators.note: after places one piece behind the other in reading order

blocks.note: a leg is one stage of a journey
dined means ate

explanation.surface: A diplomat has dinner after one stage of a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the first word and the meal follows the stage of travel, so the pieces go in that order.
explanation.definitionFit: A legate is an envoy or official representative, especially one sent by the Pope.

clue.text: Odd figure losing head is not odd

indicators.note: to lose the head is to lose the first letter

blocks.note: seven is an odd number

explanation.surface: A strange-looking person who has lost their head turns out to be perfectly normal.
explanation.walkthrough: Odd figure reads like a peculiar person, but it is an odd number; dropping its S leaves EVEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Numbers that are not odd are divisible by two, which is the meaning of even.

clue.text: Substantial aerodrome a tycoon possesses

indicators.note: to possess is to have within, so the run of letters is held inside the phrase

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A rich businessman owns a sizeable airfield.
explanation.walkthrough: The tycoon seems to be the owner in the story, but 'possesses' is the signal that the letters sit within the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Meaty means substantial or full of substance, as in a meaty argument or role.

clue.text: Pilot is US soldier on schedule with vehicle to go west

indicators.note: in an across entry, going west means running right to left

blocks.note: a rota is a schedule of duties
GI is the familiar term for an American soldier
a van is a vehicle

explanation.surface: A pilot is an American soldier on the duty roster who must drive west.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'A on B' puts A after B; the whole string is then read backwards. A rota is the British word for a duty roster.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilot in the older sense is someone who steers or guides a course, which is what a navigator does.

clue.text: Half of boys go mad for edible plant

indicators.note: half of a four-letter word is its first two letters

blocks.note: the front half of the word
to rage is to go mad with anger

explanation.surface: Some of the lads go wild for a vegetable they can eat.
explanation.walkthrough: Half of the four-letter word gives two letters; go mad is a verb giving RAGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Borage is a blue-flowered herb whose leaves and flowers are eaten in salads and drinks.

clue.text: A fight raising issue that took a while

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising lifts the letters so they read bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
a bout is a boxing or wrestling contest
to emit is to issue or give out

explanation.surface: A quarrel brings up a matter that dragged on for ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raising issue' looks like bringing up a topic, but issue is a verb and raising turns it upside down in the column.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation about time greets something that should have happened long ago, so it took a while.

clue.text: One needing no guidance to be unrefined

blocks.note: first meaning: a person with an innate talent who needs no teaching
second meaning: in its raw, unprocessed state

explanation.surface: Someone who refuses advice is bound to remain crude.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a noun for a gifted person, the second an adjective for something unprocessed, like natural sugar.
explanation.definitionFit: A gifted performer is called a natural, and raw untreated materials are described as natural.

clue.text: Cheers on swimmer in competitions on vacation

indicators.note: a vacated word has been emptied, leaving only its outside letters
in sets one group of letters within another

blocks.note: the word with all its middle letters cleared out
taken as written
a sole is a flatfish, and fish are crossword swimmers

explanation.surface: A crowd applauds a swimmer at races while on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheers looks like applause or a toast, but it is a verb meaning comforts; fish are the usual crossword swimmers.
explanation.definitionFit: To cheer someone up is to comfort them, the meaning of consoles.

clue.text: Station’s unpopular bar

blocks.note: out can mean out of favour or fashion
a post is an upright bar or pole

explanation.surface: A railway station has a pub that nobody likes.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay; bar suggests a pub but is a pole.
explanation.definitionFit: An outpost is a remote military or trading station far from the main base.

clue.text: Very small loaf last in bakery

indicators.note: last in a word means its final letter alone

blocks.note: a tin is a loaf baked in a rectangular tin, common in British bakeries
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: The final loaf left in the baker's shop is a small one.
explanation.walkthrough: A tin, or tin loaf, is a standard British bread shape baked in an oblong pan.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny is a straightforward synonym for very small or minute.

clue.text: Partners of Ant and Rik meeting for some time

blocks.note: Ant and Dec are a British TV presenting duo
Rik Mayall and Ade Edmondson were a British comedy double act

explanation.surface: The sidekicks of two comedians get together for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Partners of' governs both names: Ant and Dec host British TV shows, and Rik Mayall and Ade Edmondson starred together in The Young Ones.
explanation.definitionFit: A decade is a ten-year period, a fair stretch of time.

clue.text: Con artist puzzled after banks switch locations

indicators.note: a word's banks are its outer letters, and switching their places swaps the first with the last

blocks.note: riddled can mean puzzled or set riddles

explanation.surface: A fraudster is confused after the banks move their branches.
explanation.walkthrough: Banks look like financial institutions to suit the con artist, but they are the letters at each edge of RIDDLED.
explanation.definitionFit: A diddler is British slang for a swindler, someone who cheats people out of money.

clue.text: Repeatedly struck head getting in the hollow

indicators.note: a hollow word has had its insides removed, keeping only its edges
getting in means entering, so one part goes inside the other

blocks.note: bean is slang for the head
the first and last letters only

explanation.surface: Someone was hit again and again on the head in a hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The hollow' looks like a dip in the ground, but hollow empties the little word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaten is the past participle of beat, meaning hit over and over.

clue.text: Abridged novel so: Death of Caesar, The End

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters take on a new order
a death is a finish, so only the closing letter of the word that follows is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the closing letter of the name
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cut-down version of a novel about Julius Caesar's assassination, ending with the closing words.
explanation.walkthrough: Novel looks like a book but is the anagram signal; the fodder is SO, R and the words THE END.
explanation.definitionFit: An abridged text has been cut down in length, meaning it has been made briefer.

clue.text: Supported spy on the radio

indicators.note: things heard on the radio are only heard, so a word spelt differently will do

blocks.note: Jason Bourne is the spy hero of the Bourne novels and films

explanation.surface: A secret agent is backed up through radio broadcasts.
explanation.walkthrough: The spy is Jason Bourne, Robert Ludlum's fictional agent; his surname is pronounced the same as the definition word.
explanation.definitionFit: Borne is the past participle of bear, meaning carried or held up.

clue.text: Crew member’s blog’s funny regularly

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, taking every other letter

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters

explanation.surface: A sailor writes a blog that is always amusing.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 's is 'is', the link; the second belongs to the fodder, where every other letter is kept, starting with the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A bosun, short for boatswain, is the ship's officer in charge of the deck crew.

clue.text: The French newspaper that is socialist

blocks.note: le is French for the
FT is the Financial Times
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A French paper turns out to be left-wing.
explanation.walkthrough: The newspaper is the one this puzzle appears in, the Financial Times, abbreviated FT.
explanation.definitionFit: Leftie is an informal, often dismissive name for a person with left-wing or socialist views.

clue.text: Great performer in group beside Bill

indicators.note: beside places one piece right next to the other

blocks.note: a class is a group or category
a bill becomes an act of Parliament once passed

explanation.surface: A star turn in a band stands alongside someone called Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name, but it is draft legislation, which becomes an act.
explanation.definitionFit: A class act is an informal term for someone outstanding at what they do.

clue.text: Dealt with kind editor

blocks.note: a sort is a kind or type
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A considerate editor handled the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: Kind looks like an adjective describing the editor, but it is the noun meaning type.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorted is informal British usage for resolved or handled, so a problem dealt with is sorted.

clue.text: Relative of asp coming out of snapdragons sinuously

indicators.note: coming out of means leaving, so those letters are removed
sinuous means winding and twisting, so the letters wriggle into a new order

blocks.note: the garden flower, taken as written
the snake's three letters, which are removed from the flower

explanation.surface: A snake slithers out from among garden snapdragons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relative of asp' sounds like another snake, but the definition is just Relative; the asp is the letters to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandson is a family relation, being the son of one's child.
